rows.verified: A lithium-battery fire in an aircraft hold is a significant aviation-safety risk.
Lithium-battery incidents have involved incorrect packing, marking and labelling and misdeclared or undeclared consignments.
Batteries not transported under applicable requirements create an increased likelihood of cargo-compartment fire and potentially catastrophic consequences.
Lithium batteries must be packed, marked, labelled and documented in accordance with the ICAO Technical Instructions.
Transport of lithium batteries on their own is forbidden in the hold of passenger aircraft.
Operators should assess dangerous-goods risks through their safety-management systems and oversee contracted transport-chain activities.
Spare lithium batteries and power banks must be carried in the cabin and protected individually against short circuit.
Rules effective 27 March 2026 tighten carriage conditions for lithium cells, batteries and power banks to reduce thermal-event likelihood and impact.
Lithium-battery aviation risk depends on chemistry, capacity, manufacturing compliance, damage, packaging, declaration, stowage, detection and crew response.
CAA lithium-battery evidence is battery-, consignment-, passenger-, aircraft-, operation- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fire probability.
An Entity in Charge of Maintenance is the person or organisation responsible for the safe maintenance of a rail vehicle.
Entities in Charge of Maintenance are officially recorded in the national vehicle register.
An ECM may be a railway undertaking, infrastructure manager, vehicle keeper or maintenance organisation.
ECMs must demonstrate compliance with the applicable ROGS schedules and regulation 18A requirements.
All ECMs must comply with retained common safety methods for monitoring and for risk evaluation and assessment.
ROGS regulation 18A applies to passenger rolling stock, locomotives, freight wagons and other rail vehicles used on the mainline railway.
Entities responsible for freight-wagon maintenance require ECM certification from a competent certification body.
ORR can enforce ECM maintenance duties for mainline vehicles wherever maintenance is performed, including factories, harbours, mines and depots.
Rail-vehicle maintenance risk depends on vehicle type, duty, degradation, maintenance plan, competence, depot equipment, monitoring and return-to-service assurance.
ORR maintenance evidence is vehicle-, ECM-, task-, depot-, assurance- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level railway-failure probability.
